plan.fault: One key no longer registers or double-types because its mechanical switch has failed; replace the switch.
safety_notes: A bent pin can tear the socket's metal contact or get stuck inside it.
Do not force anything; sideways force can bend the socket's metal contacts, widen the socket, or damage the PCB.
Never push hard; a correctly aligned switch slides in with only slight smooth resistance.
Pull straight up to avoid bending the switch pins.
Static discharge can damage the controller chip on the PCB; an anti-static wrist strap is optional but recommended.
Unplug the USB-C cable before pulling switches.

steps.instruction: Disconnect the cable from the keyboard's USB-C port so the keyboard is powered down. If you have one, wear an anti-static wrist strap or touch grounded metal first.
steps.expected_visual_state: No cable is plugged into the keyboard's USB-C port and the keyboard backlight is off.
common_mistakes: Leaving the cable plugged in while pulling switches.
Reaching for the board without grounding yourself first.

steps.instruction: Hook the keycap puller's wire loops under opposite edges of the faulty key's keycap and pull straight up, then set the keycap somewhere safe. For the space bar, lift both ends evenly so the stabilizer ends release together.
steps.expected_visual_state: The keycap is off and set aside; the bare mechanical switch with its cross-shaped stem sits in the plate at the faulty key position.
common_mistakes: Pulling the wrong keycap; double-check it is the faulty key.
Pulling the keycap at an angle, which stresses the switch stem or scratches the keycap or case.
Yanking one end of the space bar so it catches on the stabilizer.
Losing the keycap.

steps.instruction: Place the switch puller's prongs on the top and bottom (north and south) clips of the switch, down where the switch meets the plate.
steps.expected_visual_state: The switch puller's two prongs rest on the top and bottom edges of the switch at plate level, not on the left and right sides.
common_mistakes: Gripping the left and right sides instead of the top and bottom clips, so the switch won't release.
Placing the prongs high on the switch housing instead of down at the plate where the clips are.
Gripping only one clip, so the switch stays locked in the plate.

steps.instruction: Gently squeeze until the clips give, then pull the switch straight up in one steady motion out of the plate and hot-swap socket. If it is stuck, stop and recheck the grip rather than yanking or rocking it.
steps.expected_visual_state: The old switch is held in the puller and an empty square hole in the plate shows the hot-swap socket on the PCB underneath.
common_mistakes: Rocking or wiggling the switch sideways while pulling, which damages the hot-swap socket.
Pulling at an angle instead of vertically.
Squeezing so hard the switch housing cracks.
Prying the switch out with fingernails.
Yanking a stuck switch without the clips released.

steps.instruction: Look into the empty hole and check the hot-swap socket is seated, undamaged and free of dust; clear debris with compressed air if needed.
steps.expected_visual_state: Through the empty plate hole, the hot-swap socket's two pin holes are clearly visible, with no debris and no lifted or damaged socket.
common_mistakes: Not noticing a damaged or lifted socket, which would make a new switch fail too.
Inserting the new switch over debris.

steps.instruction: Take a spare compatible switch, press its stem a few times to confirm it springs back, and check that both metal pins are straight and parallel; gently straighten a bent pin with tweezers.
steps.expected_visual_state: The underside of the new switch shows two straight metal pins pointing straight down, parallel to each other, with no bends.
common_mistakes: Installing a switch with a bent pin.
Bending a pin back too hard and snapping it, or using a switch with a weak or broken pin.
Using a 5-pin switch in a board that only has holes for 3-pin switches.

steps.instruction: Hold the switch over the empty hole, facing the same way as its neighbours, and line its pins up with the two socket holes, lowering it until the pins just touch the socket.
steps.expected_visual_state: The new switch sits level in the plate opening, oriented the same as the neighbouring switches, not yet pressed in.
common_mistakes: Inserting the switch rotated so the pins don't line up with the socket holes.
Holding the switch tilted so one pin goes in before the other.

steps.instruction: Press straight down evenly across the top of the switch until it clicks flush into the plate. If you feel gritty resistance or need much force, stop, remove it, and recheck the pins and socket.
steps.expected_visual_state: The new switch sits flush in the plate at the same height as its neighbours, with no gap or tilt.
common_mistakes: Forcing a misaligned switch or one with crooked pins, crushing a pin or damaging the socket.
Pressing on one side or corner only so it seats crooked.
Not pressing until it clicks, leaving the switch sitting high.

steps.instruction: Press the switch stem several times and look from the side to confirm it springs back smoothly, doesn't wobble, and stays flush.
steps.expected_visual_state: The switch top is level with neighbouring switches and its stem returns to the same resting height after each press.
common_mistakes: Skipping this check; a tilted switch usually signals a bent or misseated pin.

steps.instruction: Line up the keycap with the switch stem and press it straight down until fully seated. For the space bar, hook the stabilizers first, then press both ends down evenly.
steps.expected_visual_state: The keycap is back in its position, at the same height and angle as the surrounding keycaps.
common_mistakes: Putting the keycap on rotated or on the wrong key position.
Not seating the keycap fully so it sits higher than the others.

steps.instruction: Plug the cable back into the USB-C port and press the repaired key repeatedly in a text editor or online keyboard tester to confirm it registers exactly once per press.
steps.expected_visual_state: Cable plugged into the USB-C port, backlight on, and the screen shows the repaired key's character appearing once per press.
common_mistakes: Not testing the specific repaired key.
Not checking for double-typing by pressing the key repeatedly.

decision.why: The part costs 6.94 vs 45.11 for a new one (15% of the price).

options.badge: ✓ Fits your Royal Kludge RK61 · 4 sources
options.why: Gateron says the Kangaroo Ink switches (59gf/63gf) fit most 5-pin MX mechanical keyboards, and Royal Kludge says the RK61 accepts any compatible 3-pin or 5-pin switch with no soldering; older non-hot-swap RK61 revisions may not accept them.

options.part: GATERON G Pro 3.0 pre-lubed 5-pin RGB linear switches, Red, 35 pcs
options.badge: ✓ Fits your Royal Kludge RK61 · 4 sources
options.why: The part is a standard 5-pin MX-style switch (Gateron says G Pro 3.0 fits any 3-pin/5-pin MX keyboard), and Royal Kludge's store says the RK61 accepts any compatible 3-pin or 5-pin mechanical switch, though a Reddit post notes some older RK61 versions are not hot-swappable.

options.part: RK x LTC Kailh Switches White for Mechanical Gaming Keyboard DIY (30 Pcs, White)
options.badge: ✓ Fits your Royal Kludge RK61 · 3 sources
options.why: The part is a standard 3-pin MX cross-stem Kailh Box switch, and RTINGS and the RK store say the RK61 is hot-swappable and accepts any 3-pin or 5-pin switch, though older RK61 units with soldered switches (per GadgetExplained and Keybumps) would not accept it without desoldering.
